Setting: Academic Medical Center and Physical Medicine & Rehabili-
tation Clinic.
Results: After discharge, she struggled to progress and eventually
declined in function several months later. She returned to clinic for
her 6-month follow-up, and MRI of the cervical spine was ordered. No
abnormality on imaging explained her decline, and she was instructed
to go to the emergency department for further neurologic work-up. On
examination, she exhibited new dysarthria, much weaker strength,
diffuse muscular atrophy, and fasciculations. An electrodiagnostic
study demonstrated ﬁndings of deﬁnite amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
(ALS) according to the El Escorial criteria with upper and lower motor
neuron ﬁndings in 4 of 4 areas (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and
lumbosacral).
Discussion: The patient’s deﬁcits were initially attributed to lumbar
radiculopathy and cervical spinal stenosis. Her decline in function
several months later along with speech dysfunction prompted addi-
tional testing with an electrodiagnostic study revealing a diagnosis of
deﬁnite ALS.
Conclusions: Early ALS may be confused with other diagnoses such as
cervical myelopathy. Careful correlation of electrodiagnostic data
with clinical ﬁndings is necessary to prevent mis-diagnosis of ALS,
prevent potentially harmful procedures, and initiate timely
interventions.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 315
Complications Associated with Hajdu-Cheney
Syndrome: A Case Report
Daun Chung, DO (Baylor Institute for Rehabilitation, Dallas, Texas,
United States)
Disclosures: Daun Chung: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships
To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 28-year-old woman with history of
Hajdu-Cheney syndrome (HCS) presented with increased weakness,
numbness below T3 dermatome and spasticity leading to functional
decline. Patient had history of a syrinx formation in the cervical spinal
cord which underwent a wicking procedure sixteen years ago in
addition to multiple spine surgeries due to disease speciﬁc complica-
tions. Patient currently functions as an incomplete tetraplegic.
Setting: Acute Inpatient Rehabilitation Hospital.
Results: Magnetic Resonance Imaging of her spine showed a new
large syrinx through most of her thoracic spinal cord along with
multiple arachnoid cysts in her upper cervical and mid-thoracic
spinal cord. She underwent a partial removal of thoracic portion of
spinal instrumentation, T1-8 laminectomy and wicking of the syrinx
with a syringosubarachnoid shunt. She spent ten days in inpatient
rehabilitation for spasticity management and to improve her func-
tion. Unfortunately, patient had poor tolerance to oral anti-spas-
ticity medications and only tolerated low doses of diazepam that
provided minimal improvement in spasticity. On discharge, she was
referred to a neurosurgeon to determine candidacy for a baclofen
pump trial.
Discussion: HCS is an extremely rare disease that can be inherited as
an autosomal dominant trait or caused by gene mutation. This disease
is characterized by acroosteolysis, severe osteoporosis, skull de-
formities, and short stature. Spinal complications include compression
fractures, scoliosis, and platybasia which all contribute to spinal cord
compression. One of the major complications with HCS is basilar
invagination, which is seen in about 50% of cases and leads to a clinical
picture similar to Chiari malformation.
Conclusions: There are less than 100 cases of HCS reported in liter-

ature. These patients are at risk for multiple complications, including
spinal cord compression and syrinx formation due to spine instability
and basilar invaginations that can lead to multiple neurological com-
plications, central respiratory failure or sudden death.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 316
How a Flexible Differential Yielded an Elusive
Diagnosis: A Case Report
Kimberly Ross, MD, MBA (University of Miami Miller School of
Medicine / Jackson Memorial Hospital, Miami, FL, United States),
Alexander Harrington, MBA, Seema R. Khurana, DO
Disclosures: Kimberly Ross: I Have No Relevant Financial Relationships
To Disclose
Case/Program Description: A 48-year-old woman had initial symp-
toms of intermittent sharp lumbar pain radiating down bilateral legs,
that was unresponsive to various analgesics. This progressed to
weakness, spasticity, and immobility. After 3 years, she presented
with worsening leg pain, episodic spasms, and frequent falls. On
physical examination she had increased tone and reﬂexes of the
bilateral lower extremities. She was admitted to the hospital because
of unremitting debilitating pain.
Setting: Major urban county hospital.
Results: MRI of the spine and brain were grossly benign. Lack of sig-
niﬁcant radiographic or laboratory ﬁndings suggested an autoimmune,
paraneoplastic, myelopathic, or psychiatric etiology. She was given
trials of gabapentin, intravenous morphine, and baclofen without any
signiﬁcant relief. This lack of response prompted a suspicion of stiff
person syndrome (SPS). A trial of diazepam ultimately led to
improvement of symptoms and increased mobility. She was found to be
positive for anti-GAD-65 antibodies, which is speciﬁc for SPS, helping
to establish the diagnosis.
Discussion: SPS is a rare neuromuscular disease characterized by
baseline muscular rigidity with superimposed episodes of spasms.
Axial musculature is affected ﬁrst with extension to the proximal
limbs resulting in impaired ambulation. The estimated prevalence is
1:1,000,000, although this is likely due to underdiagnosis. Average
ages of symptom onset and diagnosis are 35 and 41.2 years, respec-
tively. Signiﬁcant impairment due to disease progression may be
prevented with earlier diagnosis. Recognizing the signs and symp-
toms, as well as subsequently ordering appropriate laboratory studies
and neuromuscular analyses can help to solidify this elusive
diagnosis.
Conclusions: Currently there is an average delay of 6.2 years between
symptom onset and diagnosis of SPS. Education of healthcare providers
about rare conditions will help to have disorders such as SPS in the
differential, which will yield more timely diagnosis and treatment, and
thus better prognosis and quality of life for affected patients.
Level of Evidence: Level V
Poster 317
Dose-Related Response to Ultrasound-Guided Ulnar
In-Plane Median Nerve Steroid Injections for Carpal
Tunnel Syndrome: A Case Report
Richard Zhang, MD (VA Greater LA Health Care System/UCLA, Los
Angeles, CA, United States), Gabriel Rudd-Barnard, MD, MS,
Lindsay M. Szafranski, DO, Ian D. Dworkin, MD, Sunny Sharma, MD,
Edward Pang, DO, MS, Dixie R. Aragaki, MD, Aashna Basu, MD
Disclosures: Richard Zhang: I Have No Relevant Financial Relation-
ships To Disclose
Case/Program Description: Patient: 36-year-old man with bilateral
carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS). Case Description: The patient endorsed
numbness
and tingling in bilateral hands, worse on the right. Physical

exam and electrodiagnostic studies were consistent with mild CTS. At
separate visits, an ultrasound-guided carpal tunnel corticosteroid in-
jection (CSI) using the ulnar-in-plane approach was performed for each
wrist (right received 20mg triamcinolone acetonide with 1.5mL 1%
lidocaine; left received 40mg triamcinolone acetonide with 1.0mL 1%
lidocaine).
Setting: Tertiary care hospital.
